summary: Dibucaine (cinchocaine) is a potent, long-acting amide local anesthetic available as a topical cream or ointment, used for the temporary relief of pain and itching due to minor burns, sunburn, insect bites, minor skin irritations, and hemorrhoids/anorectal disorders. It works by blocking sodium channels in cutaneous nerve endings. It is for external use only and should not be swallowed or applied to large areas of broken or inflamed skin, because systemic absorption can cause local-anesthetic toxicity - CNS effects (excitation then depression, seizures) and cardiovascular effects (hypotension, arrhythmia). Dibucaine is one of the more toxic local anesthetics if absorbed or ingested, and accidental pediatric ingestion of dibucaine ointment has caused serious poisoning and death; it must be kept away from children. Do not exceed the recommended amount or frequency.

moa: Dibucaine is an amide-type local anesthetic. It reversibly binds to and blocks voltage-gated sodium channels on the internal surface of the nerve cell membrane, preventing sodium influx and thereby inhibiting depolarization, impulse initiation and conduction along sensory nerve fibers. This produces a localized loss of sensation (analgesia and reduction of itch) in the area of application. It is among the most potent and longest-acting of the local anesthetics; its high potency also means a comparatively low margin of safety if absorbed systemically.

preg: Systemic absorption from appropriate topical use is minimal. There are limited data on topical dibucaine in pregnancy; pregnant women should consult a healthcare professional before use and apply only as directed.
lact: Systemic exposure from topical use is low. If used while breastfeeding, avoid applying to or near the nipple/breast immediately before nursing and consult a healthcare professional.
renal: No dose adjustment is needed for renal impairment with topical use because systemic absorption is minimal when used as directed.
hepatic: Amide local anesthetics are metabolized in the liver. With normal topical use systemic exposure is minimal; use caution with extensive application in patients with significant hepatic impairment.

missed: Dibucaine is used as needed for symptom relief, so there is no fixed dosing schedule to miss. Apply when symptoms occur, up to the maximum recommended frequency. Do not apply extra to make up for a missed application.
overdose: Excessive topical application, application to large/broken areas, or ingestion (especially by children) can cause systemic local-anesthetic toxicity: CNS excitation (restlessness, tremor, seizures) followed by CNS depression (drowsiness, respiratory depression, coma), and cardiovascular effects (hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest). There is no specific oral antidote. Management is supportive: secure airway and ventilation, control seizures with benzodiazepines, support circulation, and consider intravenous lipid emulsion therapy for severe systemic local-anesthetic toxicity. Seek emergency care after any ingestion.
